topic: Practice before the IRS and practitioner duties

notes.front: What is practice before the IRS?
notes.back: All matters connected with a presentation to the IRS about a taxpayer’s rights, privileges or liabilities under the laws and regulations it administers.
notes.explanation: Section 10.2 lists examples of such presentations, including preparing and filing documents and representing a client at conferences, hearings and meetings.
notes.example: Like an adviser writing to the IRS to dispute a client’s balance due, or sitting beside the client at an examination meeting.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 1 July 2025 edition, “§ 10.2 Definitions”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Service comprehends all matters

notes.front: What is Treasury Department Circular No. 230?
notes.back: The regulations governing practice before the IRS, published at 31 C.F.R. Subtitle A, Part 10 and released digitally as Circular 230.
notes.explanation: Publication 947 gives both names for the same rules; this deck quotes them from the 1 July 2025 printed edition of the Code of Federal Regulations.
notes.example: Like a professional code of conduct for tax representatives, but written as federal regulations.
notes.source: Publication 947 (Rev. February 2018), Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney, “What Are the Rules of Practice?”, p. 6

notes.front: What is an enrolled agent (EA)?
notes.back: Enrolled agent (EA): a person who has earned the privilege of representing taxpayers before the IRS, generally unrestricted as to clients, matters and IRS offices.
notes.explanation: The IRS puts enrolled agents alongside attorneys and certified public accountants as generally unrestricted representatives.
notes.example: Like a tax lawyer’s right to appear before any IRS office, but earned through the IRS’s own examination rather than a state bar.
notes.source: Enrolled agents frequently asked questions (IRS.gov), “Information about enrolled agents”
notes.evidence: An enrolled agent is a person who has earned the privilege of representing taxpayers before the Internal Revenue Service. Enrolled agents, like attorneys and certified public accountants (CPAs), are generally unrestricted as to which taxpayers they can represent, what types of tax matters they can handle, and which IRS offices they can represent clients before.

notes.front: What is an enrolled retirement plan agent (ERPA)?
notes.back: Enrolled retirement plan agent (ERPA): someone enrolled under Circular 230 whose practice is limited to certain retirement-plan programmes and forms.
notes.explanation: Section 10.3(e) names the Employee Plans Determination Letter programme, the Employee Plans Compliance Resolution System and the Master and Prototype and Volume Submitter programme.
notes.example: Like an EA, but confined to retirement-plan matters such as a plan’s determination letter request.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 1 July 2025 edition, “§ 10.3 Who may practice”, p. 4

notes.front: What is a preparer tax identification number (PTIN)?
notes.back: Preparer tax identification number (PTIN): the number anyone preparing federal returns for pay must hold, valid for the year, before preparing returns.
notes.explanation: The IRS adds that all enrolled agents must also have a valid PTIN.
notes.example: Like a yearly registration a paid preparer renews each season; holding one does not make the preparer an EA.
notes.source: PTIN requirements for tax return preparers (IRS.gov)
notes.evidence: Anyone who prepares or assists in preparing federal tax returns for compensation must have a valid 2026 PTIN before preparing returns. All enrolled agents must also have a valid PTIN.

notes.front: What is an enrollment cycle?
notes.back: The three successive enrolment years before the effective date of an EA’s or ERPA’s renewal; each enrolment year runs 1 January to 31 December.
notes.explanation: Section 10.6(e) uses the cycle and its years to count the continuing education needed for renewal.
notes.example: Like a three-year budget period with a minimum spend in every single year, but measured in hours of study.

notes.front: What is continuing education (CE) for an enrolled agent?
notes.back: Continuing education (CE): qualifying study an EA must certify completing, in the required number of hours, to qualify for renewal.
notes.explanation: For an EA, a qualifying programme must be designed to enhance professional knowledge in Federal taxation or Federal tax related matters.
notes.example: Like the training hours many licensed professionals log to keep practising.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 1 July 2025 edition, “§ 10.6(e) Condition for renewal: continuing education”, p. 9

notes.front: What does Circular 230 say about an unconscionable fee?
notes.back: A practitioner may not charge an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the IRS.
notes.explanation: Section 10.27(a) sets no amount or formula; it bars such a fee for any matter before the IRS.

notes.front: When does a conflict of interest exist under Circular 230?
notes.back: When representing one client is directly adverse to another, or significantly risks being materially limited by duties to others or the practitioner’s own interest.
notes.explanation: The duties that can limit the representation may be owed to another client, a former client or a third person.
notes.example: Like one adviser acting for both the buyer and the seller of a business on how the price is taxed.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 1 July 2025 edition, “§ 10.29 Conflicting interests”, p. 19
